The slot-inactive condition is NOT a 14:34Z onset but a long-running pre-existing state: the WARN 'retaining <n> MB of WAL' pattern runs continuously from 13:02:25Z (33247 MB) through 13:12:19Z (77137 MB), 13:37:25Z (37927 MB), 13:48:09Z (92599 MB), 13:52:50Z (82259 MB), 14:16:25Z (78423 MB)... to 14:49:47Z (77371 MB), i.e. at least 1h32m before the release, with retained WAL oscillating in the tens of GB the whole time.

The ledger-db write path died on storage capacity with the same signature as the reported symptom, and continued past the rollback: 153 ERROR lines of 'PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.<n>": No space left on device' spanning 15:01:01Z to 16:57:21Z (tc-054 top_patterns and tc-036). With no analytics/CDC service in the catalog and no slot drop/activation/retention-cap log at ledger-db, the origin hop of H1 (what stopped the WAL consumer at ~14:34Z) is unobservable in the available telemetry: there is neither a consumer-side event nor a slot-maintenance event to close the chain. This shifts the fix target to ledger-db-side WAL/slot retention (a slot with no managed/known consumer) rather than an incident-driven consumer outage.

events.summary: H1 is the only hypothesis that survives scrutiny, and every hop from the disk-fill onward is verified rather than assumed: ledger-db /var/lib/postgresql/data climbs monotonically 94.73% (14:00Z) -> 97.85% (14:35Z) -> 98% (14:48:20Z) -> pinned 100.0 from the 14:56Z bucket (F9,F16,F26); the WARN 'replication slot analytics_cdc is inactive; retaining <n> MB of WAL' runs continuously from 13:02:25Z with retained volume oscillating in the tens of GB (F37,F24,F29); PostgreSQL PANICs on WAL writes ('could not write to file pg_wal/xlogtemp... No space left on device', 153 lines, 15:01:01Z-16:57:21Z) (F38,F28); payment-service surfaces the identical ENOSPC (354 ERROR lines, first 15:00:26Z) (F8,F18); and order-service fails independently on 'INSERT INTO orders ... No space left on device' (F10), which no payment-service code path can explain. Temporal order is tight and favorable: retention announced well before the incident, disk 98% at 14:48:20Z, error-rate step at 14:54-14:58Z, first payment write error 15:00:26Z - cause precedes onset. Alternatives are eliminated on evidence, not assertion: the rollback test shows no recovery with storage still pinned at 100% and PANICs continuing (F27,F28), which kills H2/H5; MANDATE_HOLD and entry_type match 0 log lines everywhere (F20,F21) so the contract mechanism has no telemetry support; flat p99 (~293-348ms), flat request_rate (~100 req/s), flat CPU (~30%) and flat slow_queries (~1/min) exclude load, latency and query-cost families (F11,F14,F15,F17); H3 is unverifiable (F6) and contradicted by shared ENOSPC + order-service collateral; H4 has no audit surface at all - get_config_changes and get_deployments both return count=0 for ledger-db with no independent parameter/tuning surface existing (F30-F34), so it is documentably out of scope, not a live competitor, and its hypothetical trigger is also less parsimonious than the retention condition already logged from 13:02:25Z. The origin hop (why the slot's WAL consumer left) remains unobservable by construction - there is no analytics/CDC service in the catalog and no slot-active/WAL-bytes metric (F35,F39) - but this is a secondary detail of an otherwise established origin, and the decisive fix step (reclaim the ledger-db volume, restore WAL recycling, drop the unmanaged orphan slot) does not depend on it. Two refinements to keep the claim honest: the precise retention onset is not pinned by the lag series (F25 shows only a slow pre-existing trend), and payment-service v6.0.0 is not positively exonerated as a transient WAL-generation accelerant into an already-filling volume - neither changes the identified fault or the fix target.

If legacy paths fail at the same ~60%, H2 is dead and H1 is confirmed; if failures concentrate exclusively on MANDATE_HOLD, H1's scope claim is wrong. It is the one discrimination attempt that was killed by budget rather than answered.

evidence_requests.question: For ledger-db, retrieve replication-slot/WAL state: replication_lag_ms across 14:00Z–16:59Z, disk/WAL growth onset, and any metric or log line indicating when a replication slot became inactive or a WAL consumer stopped around 14:30–14:36Z (the point WAL was already 33916 MB at 14:34:05Z). Also report whether disk_used_pct or errors changed after the 15:12Z rollback.
evidence_requests.rationale: Grounds (or falsifies) H1's unverified origin hop — that an inactive replication slot is retaining WAL — and identifies the trigger event; also tests whether the 15:12Z release rollback altered the error rate, which would discriminate the release hypothesis from the storage hypothesis.

critiques.summary: H1 is the only hypothesis that survives scrutiny and its core mechanism (ledger-db volume full -> ENOSPC -> writes blocked) is verified at every hop from the disk-fill onward. The temporal order is now tight and favorable: WAL retention announced 14:34:05Z, disk 98% at 14:48:20Z, error-rate step at 14:54-14:58Z, first payment ledger-write error 15:00:26Z — the cause precedes onset. Scope is explained: order-service's independent INSERT INTO orders fails on the identical ENOSPC (F10), which no payment-service code fault can explain, and the rollback test (F27/F28) plus flat p99/request_rate/CPU/slow_queries (F11,F14,F15,F17) eliminate the contract-fault and latency/load families. H2/H5 are contradicted by the absence of any validator/constraint error and the 0-match MANDATE_HOLD/entry_type filters (F20,F21); H3 is unverifiable (F6) and contradicted by ENOSPC + order-service collateral; H4 is contradicted by F2 and by the fact that no config change could produce WAL growth beginning at 14:34Z more parsimoniously than the slot-inactive condition already logged. Two blocking gaps remain, both cheap and obtainable, both capable of changing the ranking or the confidence: (1) the ORIGIN hop — the inactive 'analytics_cdc' slot is asserted from three WARN lines (F24,F29) while replication_lag_ms shows a pre-existing ~3.1-3.5s trend with NO step at 14:34Z (F25), so what actually started WAL retention at 14:34Z is unresolved and the alternative "WAL growth is itself the symptom of something else" was never positively excluded; (2) the rollout nested within the WAL/disk series is fully consistent with H1 but the one competing fine-grained mechanism — did the disk fill happen FIRST (H1) or did a same-window WAL-retention configuration/consumer-stop event coincide with a deploy-driven write surge — was never isolated because the consumer side of the slot was never queried and get_config_changes coverage is unknown. Note that the contract-vs-storage discrimination (T4) is now settled negatively: telemetry physically lacks the entry_type/route fields (F19,F21,F23), so re-requesting the per-entry-type split would be repeating a request that has already failed for a permanent reason; I do not ask for it again. Capping confidence at 0.72.

challenges.issue: Origin hop is asserted, not evidenced: the 'analytics_cdc' slot becoming inactive is read off three WARN log lines (F24,F29). The only quantitative replication series available, replication_lag_ms, was already 3.1-3.5s before 14:34Z and shows NO step at 14:34Z (F25), which means the logged slot-inactive condition is not confirmed as the moment WAL retention actually began. The consumer-side event at ~14:30-14:34Z was never queried, so 'slot stopped consuming' remains an inference from log text rather than a measured state change.

The WAL-growth hop rests on three data points (33916 -> 69518 -> 77371 MB across 14:34-14:49Z) with no WAL-bytes series and no slot-state metric (gaps explicitly note neither exists). Rapid WAL retention is consistent with an inactive slot but also with a write-rate/WAL-generation surge or a retention-setting change in the same window; the series alone cannot separate 'slot stopped recycling' from 'WAL generated faster than it was recycled'. This is a secondary/mechanism-level uncertainty, not a competing origin, so it caps confidence but does not overturn H1.

Calibration: stated confidence 0.68 is below my defensible cap, but the framing 'not the release' is stronger than the evidence supports. F1 shows dep-6203 (14:46Z) is the only change across ALL services in-window and F4 shows it precedes the 14:55Z onset by ~9 minutes. Its rollback at 15:12Z changed nothing (F27,F28), which falsifies it as the CONTINUING cause but not necessarily as a contributing WAL-surge driver that accelerated an already-climbing fill (94.73% at 14:00Z, climbing throughout). H1 should be worded as 'storage exhaustion is the dominant, ongoing cause; the deploy is neither necessary nor sufficient', which the data supports, rather than asserting the deploy played no role at all.

H4 remains a live category-level alternative only because get_config_changes returned count=0 with unknown coverage (F2). Zero results from an API of unverified coverage cannot positively exclude an unrecorded retention/slot-cleanup config change, and such a change would be a distinct fix target (config revert) from volume reclamation. Needs either a direct ledger-db configuration audit or an explicit statement that no such audit surface exists.

Contradiction is now airtight on mechanism (no validator/constraint error; identical ENOSPC hits order-service; ENOSPC persists after rollback), but the direct endpoint-level falsification (mandate routes vs legacy routes failing at the same rate) was never obtained and cannot be — the fields do not exist (F19,F21,F23). H2 is correctly rejected on the evidence available; this is a note that its rejection is inferential rather than a direct A/B measurement, which is acceptable given the telemetry.

evidence_requests.question: Identify the consumer that owns ledger-db's replication slot 'analytics_cdc' and determine what happened to it at ~14:30-14:34Z: query the analytics/CDC consumer service's own logs and metrics (liveness, restarts, error rate, throughput, connection status) over 14:00Z-15:00Z. Did that consumer stop, crash, restart, or get disabled around 14:30-14:34Z, and is there any ledger-db-side log line naming the slot being dropped/activated/deactivated or a retention cap being hit (beyond the three WARN lines already found)? If no such consumer service exists in the catalog, say so explicitly.
evidence_requests.rationale: This is the single blocking gap. H1's origin hop ('slot stops consuming, so WAL is retained') is currently an inference from three WARN lines, while replication_lag_ms shows no step at 14:34Z (F25). If the consumer crashed/stopped at 14:30-14:34Z, H1's causal chain is closed end-to-end and confidence can go to ~0.85. If no consumer event exists, then WAL growth is unexplained at its origin and H1's trigger is mis-specified (the disk-fill/blast-radius conclusions still stand, but the fix target shifts from 'slot maintenance' to 'find what began retaining WAL'), which changes the recommended action.

evidence_requests.question: Audit ledger-db's own configuration and WAL-retention settings for changes in 14:00Z-15:10Z through a source other than get_config_changes (which returned count=0 with unknown coverage): is there any ledger-db configuration history, parameter-change log, or infrastructure/tuning record showing a change to max_wal_size, wal_keep_size, replication slot retention, archive_command, or slot cleanup timing in that window? Explicitly report whether such an audit surface EXISTS at all; if it does not, state that get_config_changes has no coverage for datastore-level configuration and the question is unanswerable rather than negative.
evidence_requests.rationale: Disambiguates H1 vs H4. H4 is live solely because a zero result from an API of unknown coverage cannot exclude an unrecorded retention-setting change, which would be a different fix (config revert). This is a bounded, obtainable audit; if the surface truly does not exist, the team should document it and stop treating H4 as live.

critiques.summary: H1 is the only hypothesis that survives scrutiny, and every hop from the disk-fill onward is verified rather than assumed: ledger-db /var/lib/postgresql/data climbs monotonically 94.73% (14:00Z) -> 97.85% (14:35Z) -> 98% (14:48:20Z) -> pinned 100.0 from the 14:56Z bucket (F9,F16,F26); the WARN 'replication slot analytics_cdc is inactive; retaining <n> MB of WAL' runs continuously from 13:02:25Z with retained volume oscillating in the tens of GB (F37,F24,F29); PostgreSQL PANICs on WAL writes ('could not write to file pg_wal/xlogtemp... No space left on device', 153 lines, 15:01:01Z-16:57:21Z) (F38,F28); payment-service surfaces the identical ENOSPC (354 ERROR lines, first 15:00:26Z) (F8,F18); and order-service fails independently on 'INSERT INTO orders ... No space left on device' (F10), which no payment-service code path can explain. Temporal order is tight and favorable: retention announced well before the incident, disk 98% at 14:48:20Z, error-rate step at 14:54-14:58Z, first payment write error 15:00:26Z - cause precedes onset. Alternatives are eliminated on evidence, not assertion: the rollback test shows no recovery with storage still pinned at 100% and PANICs continuing (F27,F28), which kills H2/H5; MANDATE_HOLD and entry_type match 0 log lines everywhere (F20,F21) so the contract mechanism has no telemetry support; flat p99 (~293-348ms), flat request_rate (~100 req/s), flat CPU (~30%) and flat slow_queries (~1/min) exclude load, latency and query-cost families (F11,F14,F15,F17); H3 is unverifiable (F6) and contradicted by shared ENOSPC + order-service collateral; H4 has no audit surface at all - get_config_changes and get_deployments both return count=0 for ledger-db with no independent parameter/tuning surface existing (F30-F34), so it is documentably out of scope, not a live competitor, and its hypothetical trigger is also less parsimonious than the retention condition already logged from 13:02:25Z. The origin hop (why the slot's WAL consumer left) remains unobservable by construction - there is no analytics/CDC service in the catalog and no slot-active/WAL-bytes metric (F35,F39) - but this is a secondary detail of an otherwise established origin, and the decisive fix step (reclaim the ledger-db volume, restore WAL recycling, drop the unmanaged orphan slot) does not depend on it. Two refinements to keep the claim honest: the precise retention onset is not pinned by the lag series (F25 shows only a slow pre-existing trend), and payment-service v6.0.0 is not positively exonerated as a transient WAL-generation accelerant into an already-filling volume - neither changes the identified fault or the fix target.

challenges.issue: The origin hop is not verified: what stopped or orphaned the analytics_cdc consumer is unobservable - no analytics/CDC service exists in the catalog (F35), no slot-active/WAL-bytes metric exists, and replication_lag_ms shows only a slow pre-existing ~3.1-3.5s trend with no step at 14:34Z (F25). The retention onset instant is therefore bounded by log WARNs (13:02:25Z-14:49:47Z) rather than pinned. This caps confidence below 0.9 but does not move the fix target, which is ledger-db-side slot/WAL retention regardless of what the consumer did.

v6.0.0 is treated as 'not the ongoing cause' but is not positively exonerated as a transient write/WAL-generation contributor into an already 98%-full volume between 14:46Z and the 15:00Z error stream; no ledger-db write-rate/WAL-generation series exists to separate retention from generation, and the all-services change inventory shows dep-6203 as the only in-window change (F1,F31). This is correctly flagged as an assumption and does not alter the fix target.

H4 is categorized as an active live alternative at 0.08 despite having zero supporting findings, a fully assumed first hop, and both automated checks flagging it as unevidenced. Since no datastore parameter/retention audit surface exists at all (F34, T7), it is unverifiable rather than competitive; it should be closed as documentably out of scope rather than ranked, so it cannot later be mistaken for an untested rival origin.

Rejection of H2 is inferential rather than direct: telemetry physically lacks entry_type/route fields (F19,F21,F23), so the per-entry-type and per-route failure fractions were never measured. The rejection is nonetheless sound because it rests on independent, positive axes - an ENOSPC signature with no validator/constraint error anywhere, the same ENOSPC killing order-service's unrelated orders path (F10), no post-rollback recovery (F27), and 0 matches for MANDATE_HOLD/entry_type (F20,F21).

Full blast radius is only partially quantified: error-rate/latency curves were not obtained for order-service, settlement-service, api-gateway or ledger-db (budget exhaustion), so scope is established by log-level collateral (F10) plus catalog sharing (F3) rather than by metric corroboration. This affects breadth-of-impact reporting, not the identified cause or fix.
